This section collects source-collection stubs for research areas relevant to the site's main topics. The individual review pages are intentionally conservative: they identify review questions and source links, but they do not yet claim to synthesize the literature.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Current status

Each review page below is still incomplete. Treat these pages as review scaffolds until they include paper-by-paper summaries, extracted evidence, and explicit limitations.
:::

## Current Review Topics

- [Interaction Forces in the Golf Swing](research-review-interaction-forces.html): source-collection stub for interaction forces, segment sequencing, and golf-specific evidence gaps.
- [Induced Acceleration Analysis](research-review-induced-acceleration-analysis.html): source-collection stub for force-contribution and acceleration-decomposition methods.
- [Baseball Pitching Biomechanics](research-review-baseball-pitching.html): source-collection stub for cross-sport comparison material relevant to multi-segment throwing motions.
- [Shaft Flexibility in Golf Swing Dynamics](research-review-shaft-flexibility.html): source-collection stub for shaft bending, stiffness, flexible-club modeling, and fitting claims.

## Editorial Intent

When these pages are completed, each review should do four things:

1. State the main question addressed in the literature.
2. Distinguish empirical findings from modeling assumptions and interpretation.
3. Explain what the cited work actually supports, and what it does not support.
4. Note where the literature bears directly on AffineDrift's claims and where it does not.

## Suggested Completion Order

1. [Induced Acceleration Analysis](research-review-induced-acceleration-analysis.html), because it is most directly relevant to force-attribution questions.
2. [Interaction Forces in the Golf Swing](research-review-interaction-forces.html), because it speaks to segment sequencing and passive/active interaction terms.
3. [Shaft Flexibility in Golf Swing Dynamics](research-review-shaft-flexibility.html), because shaft-model assumptions affect several golf-specific pages.
4. [Baseball Pitching Biomechanics](research-review-baseball-pitching.html), because it is useful mainly as a comparison domain rather than a direct golf source.
